issues.legal_issue: The statutory procedures for recovering rent or damages from occupants of government premises may apply even when the letting or occupation began before the statute came into force.
material_facts: The claim concerned damages assessed for occupation that began before the Act came into force and continued until the premises were derequisitioned.
The Court considered the Act’s procedures for recovering rent arrears and damages for unauthorised occupation.
issues.conclusion: The date on which the letting or occupation began does not by itself prevent use of the Act’s recovery procedures, provided the premises are government premises and the relevant statutory conditions for recovery are met.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4 and 6 permit recovery of rent arrears that remain payable for occupation of government premises, and section 12 permits recovery of damages where a person is in unauthorised occupation of government premises. There is no vested right to a particular procedure. The Act’s purpose and scheme therefore permit its procedures to apply to pre-commencement letting or occupation. The contrary view in Shri Sripat Rai v. District Magistrate, Banaras was incorrect.

rule.if: recovery_claim_under_statutory_procedure and government_premises and prior_commencement_occupation and (recoverable_rent_arrears or current_unauthorized_occupation)

predicates.recovery_claim_under_statutory_procedure: A party seeks recovery of rent or damages for occupation of premises through a statutory recovery procedure.
predicates.government_premises: The premises belong to, are leased by, or have been requisitioned by the government.
predicates.prior_commencement_occupation: The letting or occupation began before the recovery procedure came into force.
predicates.recoverable_rent_arrears: Rent arrears remain legally recoverable for occupation of the premises.
predicates.current_unauthorized_occupation: The person is in unauthorised occupation of the premises when the damages recovery procedure is pursued.

issues.definition: When a statutory recovery claim concerns government premises and the relevant rent arrears remain recoverable or unauthorised occupation is ongoing, occupation that began before the procedure came into force does not bar statutory recovery.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory recovery claim based on premises allegedly requisitioned by the government requires proof that the premises were validly requisitioned by an authorised authority.
material_facts: The government claimed that the premises had been requisitioned under the Defence of India Rules.
No notification containing an order of requisition under the relevant rule was produced.
The district magistrate’s purported requisition order was not valid under the rule relied on, and no delegation of the government’s requisition power to the district magistrate was shown.
The record therefore did not establish that the premises were requisitioned property or government premises.
issues.conclusion: The premises were not established on the record to be government premises, so the defendants could not recover the claimed amount under the Act.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 2(c) of the U.P. Government Premises (Rent Recovery and Eviction) Act, requisitioned premises qualify as government premises. The relevant requisition power under rule 75A of the Defence of India Rules was conferred on the government; section 2(5) of the Defence of India Act permitted delegation, but no such delegation to the district magistrate was shown. A purported order under rule 81(2)(bb) did not establish a valid requisition.

predicates.statutory_recovery_claim_based_on_requis: A party seeks statutory recovery on the basis that the premises were requisitioned by the government.
predicates.requisitioned_status_asserted: A party asserts that the premises were requisitioned property.
predicates.valid_requisition_established: The record establishes a valid requisition order made by an authority empowered to make it.

issues.definition: When statutory recovery depends on premises having been requisitioned, an assertion of requisition without an established valid requisition does not establish government-premises status for recovery.

issues.legal_issue: A respondent may rely on a ground raised below but rejected or left undecided to support a decree, so long as reliance on it does not mutilate or destroy the decree.
material_facts: The respondent relied on the ground that the premises had not been shown to be government premises.
That ground had been raised before the High Court, which did not decide it.
The respondent relied on the ground to support the decree under appeal.
issues.conclusion: The respondent was entitled to recanvass the ground in the Supreme Court to support the decree.
issues.legal_principle: On the analogy of Order 41, rule 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a party may support a decree on a ground raised and decided against that party below, or not considered below. The limitation is that the ground cannot be used to mutilate or destroy the decree.

predicates.appeal_from_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree.
predicates.respondent_seeks_to_support_decree_on_gr: The respondent relies on a ground to uphold the decree under appeal.
predicates.ground_raised_below_but_rejected_or_unco: The ground was raised below and either rejected or not decided.
predicates.reliance_does_not_mutilate_or_destroy_de: Relying on the ground would not mutilate or destroy the decree.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a decree, a respondent may recanvass a previously raised but rejected or undecided ground to support the decree if doing so would not mutilate or destroy it.
